common_name: Ebony Acorn Squash (Black-Skinned Bush Acorn Squash)

planting.note: Direct sow after all frost danger has passed and soil has warmed; the compact bush habit suits smaller gardens and needs no trellising.

directions: Ebony Acorn is an All-America Selections winner from the 1960s bred for its deep, glossy black-green rind and compact bush vines that need far less garden space than sprawling acorn types. Fruit develops the classic deeply ribbed acorn shape and matures to a dense, dry, sweet orange flesh well suited to baking or stuffing. Because the bush habit concentrates fruit near the crown, side-dress with compost partway through the season to sustain the shorter root run, and harvest once the rind hardens and resists a fingernail scratch. Cure harvested fruit in a warm, airy spot for one to two weeks before long-term storage to improve flavor and shelf life.

common_name: Rugosa Friulana Squash (Italian Bumpy-Skinned Heirloom Pumpkin)

planting.note: Direct sow in hills once soil is reliably warm; give the long, vigorous vines generous room to sprawl or train them up a sturdy support.

directions: Rugosa Friulana is a traditional Italian heirloom from the Friuli region prized for its warty, tan-beige rind and remarkably dense, sweet, deep-orange flesh, long favored in northern Italy for filling tortelli di zucca and other stuffed pastas. The pear-to-oblong fruit develops a rough, bumpy skin as it matures, a trait that distinguishes it visually from the smoother Marina di Chioggia despite both being Cucurbita moschata types from neighboring regions. Vines are vigorous and productive, so provide rich, well-drained soil and consistent moisture through fruit development, then reduce watering as the rind hardens to concentrate sugars. Cure fruit in a warm spot for a couple of weeks after harvest before storing to further develop its characteristic sweetness.

planting.note: Direct sow after soil has warmed and frost danger has passed, or start indoors 2-3 weeks early in short-season climates; allow ample space for sprawling vines.

directions: Kikuza is a Japanese heirloom kabocha-type squash bearing flattened, deeply lobed fruit with a dark green rind roughened by prominent grayish-tan warts and scarring, a distinctive look among the smoother-skinned kabocha commonly sold in supermarkets. The dry, dense flesh is deep orange-yellow and intensely sweet with the chestnut-like flavor characteristic of the finest kabocha strains, and it stores well for months when cured properly. Grow it as you would other maxima kabocha types, keeping vines evenly watered until fruit sets and then letting soil dry somewhat as the rind hardens and corking develops around the stem. Cure harvested squash in a warm, dry location for one to two weeks to toughen the skin and sweeten the flesh before storage.

planting.note: Direct sow after frost danger passes and soil has warmed; give the sprawling vines a fence or trellis to climb, or ample ground space if left to ramble.

directions: Nest Egg Gourd produces smooth, hard-shelled, egg-shaped fruit in creamy white that so closely resembles a real hen's egg it was historically tucked into nest boxes to encourage laying hens to return to the same spot. Vines are vigorous and prolific, setting numerous small gourds through the season, and the fruit dries to a durable, long-lasting shell once fully mature and cured. Harvest when the shell has hardened and resists denting, leaving a short stem attached, then cure in a warm, dry, well-ventilated spot for several weeks until lightweight and rattle-free inside. Beyond its farmyard use, it remains popular for autumn craft displays and children's garden projects because of its uncanny egg mimicry.

common_name: Tennessee Dancing Gourd (Appalachian Curved-Neck Ornamental Gourd)
scientific_name: Cucurbita pepo var. ovifera 'Tennessee Dancing Gourd'

planting.note: Direct sow once soil is warm and frost risk has passed; trellising keeps the small, oddly shaped gourds cleaner and easier to harvest.

directions: Tennessee Dancing Gourd is a small Appalachian heirloom ornamental gourd whose bulbous body tapers into a curved, off-center neck, causing the dried gourd to wobble and rock rather than sit flat when set on a table. Vines are prolific bearers of these quirky little gourds, which mature with a hard, mottled orange-and-green or cream-striped shell depending on the strain grown. Harvest once the rind has fully hardened and the stem begins to dry, then cure the gourds in a warm, airy location for several weeks until the shells are lightweight and durable. Long grown in home gardens across the southern Appalachians more for novelty and fall decoration than for any culinary use, it makes an easy, low-maintenance conversation piece for children's gardens.

common_name: Cave Man's Club Gourd (Long Clubbed Hard-Shell Gourd)

planting.note: Direct sow, or start indoors 2-3 weeks early where seasons are short, after nicking the hard seed coat to speed germination; give this vigorous climber a strong overhead trellis so the long fruit hangs straight.

directions: Cave Man's Club is a hard-shell bottle gourd selection that develops a long, heavy, swollen club shape reminiscent of a primitive weapon, with fruit commonly reaching two feet or more when grown on a sturdy overhead structure that lets it hang straight and true. Like other Lagenaria gourds, the large white night-blooming flowers open toward evening and are typically pollinated by moths, so hand-pollination with a soft brush in early morning can improve fruit set in gardens without natural pollinators active at dusk. Leave fruit on the vine until the stem browns and shrivels and the shell resists denting, then cure in a warm, dry, ventilated space for one to several months until it feels light and the seeds rattle inside. Once fully cured, the tough woody shell can be cleaned, sanded, and finished for use in traditional gourd crafts.

planting.note: Direct sow once frost danger has passed and soil has warmed; the vigorous vines can be left to ramble over a fence or bed edge.

directions: Spinning Gourd bears small, rounded fruit with a pointed, tapered base that lets a dried gourd be set on a hard surface and given a flick to spin like a top, a trait that has made it a favorite novelty gourd for children and fall craft fairs. Fruit typically colors up in mottled combinations of orange, cream, and green stripes, and vines are prolific, often producing dozens of gourds per plant over the season. Harvest once the shell hardens fully and resists a fingernail, then cure in a warm, dry, airy spot for several weeks until the gourd is lightweight with loose, rattling seeds inside. Because the fruit is small and quick to mature, it is well suited to shorter growing seasons where larger ornamental gourds may struggle to fully ripen.
